extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students studying equitable remedies for patent infringement
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when and how a court of equity should grant, dissolve, continue, or make final injunctions in patent-infringement disputes, and related remedies (accounts, inspections, referral to law courts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay / unreasonable delay by plaintiff
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff who has delayed seeking equitable relief (e.g., allowed a suit to remain dormant for years after knowledge of alleged infringement) may be refused an injunction or relief in equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court will look for satisfactory reasons why the plaintiff did not apply earlier; where no reason is shown, the court may refuse to retain a bill or grant an injunction. Long unexplained delay exposes defendants to unnecessary inconvenience (e.g., chancery suit hanging over defendant for years). If circumstances deprived plaintiff of earlier opportunity, the question may differ. Example given: plaintiffs knew of infringement in August 1835 but waited four years; court found refusal proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession and exercise of exclusive right (prima facie ground for injunction)
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain an injunction the plaintiff should generally show long possession and exercise of his exclusive right — a prima facie case of possession and enjoyment of the patent right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No fixed period is prescribed; the general principle is that time elapsed between grant and injunction must have been sufficient to permit the patentee to construct and sell articles or machines in conformity with his claim, and to sell them publicly and repeatedly. If plaintiff makes out a prima facie case by possession/enjoyment, that supports granting an injunction until further order.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the court will send the plaintiff to try title at law (no injunction initially)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the plaintiff does not show long possession and exercise of exclusive right, or if evidence casts doubt on originality, infringement, or where patent contains gross/obvious defects, the court will ordinarily require the plaintiff to establish his patent at law rather than grant an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is discretionary. The court may refuse to grant or retain an injunction and direct the plaintiff to bring an action at law to try validity or title. Where both parties claim under patents, the court generally cannot grant an injunction until the rights are tried at law.

rubrics_metrics.name: No specific temporal standard for 'long possession'
rubrics_metrics.description: No precise lapse of time has been adopted as a standard for how long possession/exercise must have continued to justify an injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although no positive rule exists, the possession must be of such duration as to permit construction and public, repeated sale of the patented articles; proof of public sale should be shown if that is the relied-upon kind of possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Former recoveries or licenses as proof of possession (subject to non-collusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof of possession may consist of former recoveries or licenses granted to parties who submitted; these can support a claim of possession and enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such recoveries/submissions will not establish the necessary possession if it appears they were collusively obtained; they need not have been obtained by trial — they remain effective if there was originally a real contest. Example: where many licenses were prepared/granted and parties submitted, court found sufficient use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Former use/recoveries must be under the same or law-connected patent
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on former use or former recoveries as proof of possession, they must have been under the same patent, or under a patent connected in law with the present patent; otherwise they will not show they related to the same right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under systems allowing amended specifications or surrendering an old patent and taking out a new one for informalities, the right in contemplation of law may remain the same and support injunctions under the amended/new patent if it is in fact the same invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunctions are interlocutory and provisional
rubrics_metrics.description: All orders granting injunctions on such applications are generally interlocutory (until further order) and do not decide the ultimate rights between the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An injunction granted 'until further order' is not perpetual; defendant may displace affidavits, both sides may proceed to evidence and hearing, and the whole case (law and facts) may be reconsidered at final hearing. The court considers whether to impose terms or other modes of investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant's right to further investigation / trial at law
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant shows questions of fact or law that equity does not ordinarily determine, he is entitled to further investigation, usually by ordering a trial at law (or directing an issue out of chancery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court will consider whether the nature of the case entitles defendant to a further investigation; where such questions exist, an action at law will generally be ordered, though a chancery issue is competent. The defendant's option to have the matter tried at law is commonly respected; courts exercise fair discretion in this choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to specify prior use details when seeking issue out of chancery
rubrics_metrics.description: If the defendant wishes to try the question of originality by an issue out of chancery, he must set out in his answer the names of places and persons where and by whom the invention was previously used, as required by the Act of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a peremptory statutory requirement for trials at law of originality; it has been held that failure to provide such particulars will prevent trying originality by issue out of chancery. (Query noted whether court ordering defendant to file the notice before issue tried would suffice.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendency of action against another party is not alone sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere fact that an action is pending against another party is not sufficient ground for continuing an injunction where the novelty of the invention is denied in the answer, without compelling the plaintiff to bring an action against the new defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court expects the plaintiff to be put to his action against the other defendant if novelty is denied; pendency alone does not justify continued equitable relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for dissolving, reviving, or continuing injunctions follow same principles as granting them
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions to dissolve an injunction (or to revive/continue it) are decided on the same principles as the original grant: the defendant cannot displace plaintiff's prima facie right merely by filing an answer or affidavits casting doubt, provided plaintiff has not unreasonably delayed and adduces supporting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a motion to dissolve is made after a trial at law has been ordered or while an action is pending, court looks to same principles; where trial results are not final (e.g., rule nisi for new trial pending), court will seek to place parties in situation minimizing inconvenience and may withhold continuation of injunction as matter of course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of a trial at law on equitable relief
rubrics_metrics.description: After a trial at law, the court will consider the result; if proceedings at law are not final (e.g., new trial may be granted), the court may not simply continue or dissolve injunction as a matter of course but will consider remaining questions and overall convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: verdict for plaintiff followed by motion for new trial — court may refuse to continue injunction automatically; it will weigh inconvenience to parties, possible outcomes at law, and whether to direct account or other measures pending finality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of profits as an alternative or adjunct to injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: An account of profits made by the defendant may be ordered in lieu of granting/continuing an injunction, and is always ordered when the injunction is made perpetual unless the amount would be very small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounts during pendency preserve plaintiff's ability to obtain full relief if ultimately entitled, and are ordered especially where defendant might make new contracts. An account may also be ordered if injunction is dissolved because it would do irreparable injury to defendant's business. Where injunction is dissolved pending law proceedings, court often orders defendant to keep an account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual inspection of works to facilitate trial
rubrics_metrics.description: When an action at law is to be tried on the question of infringement, the court may order mutual inspection of the plaintiff's and defendant's works so that parties can present appropriate evidence at trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is used as a practical step to enable factual proof on infringement at the subsequent trial; ordered as a further means of doing justice between the parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core patent-validity requirements referenced for equitable consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of equitable relief and the law on patents generally: (1) the invention must be novel; (2) it must be useful; (3) the specification must be intelligible; and (4) the specification must not attempt to claim more than the patentee is strictly entitled to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These matters (utility, intelligibility, novelty) are for jury as facts; whether specification attempts to cover too much is a question of law to be considered by courts. A patent that attempts to cover more than its real discovery — e.g., claiming original invention where only a particular combination or application was discovered — may be rendered ineffectual even to the extent it would otherwise be valid. Conversely, valid patents may exist for new combinations/applications of previously used materials if the specification clearly confines claim to that combination/application only.
